sentences.text: Argentinonectes is estimated to have measured between 7 and 9 m in total length, with forelimbs about 1.8 m long and hindlimbs about 1.3 m long.
Its dorsal vertebrae possess T-shaped transverse processes, and the humerus displays a pronounced sigmoid curve and an expanded inner base for articulation with the ulna.
The hand bones are spool-shaped and feature polygonal surfaces where they connect.
The ribs and gastralia are pachyostotic, a thickening that would have helped the animal stay buoyant in the water.
Shark teeth belonging to Protosqualus argentinensis, Notidanodon (or Xampylodon) dentatus, and Echinorhinus maremagnum were recovered close to the holotype.
Parallel scratches on the coracoid are interpreted as marks left by scavenging sharks shedding teeth.
A partial articulated skeleton was uncovered in 2009 beneath 50 cm of water in Lake Argentino, Argentina.
The excavation and study were led by Fernando Novas, and the specimen is curated as MPM-PV 10.004 in the Padre Manuel Jesús Molina Provincial Regional Museum.
The genus Argentinonectes was formally named by Novas et al. in 2026.
To date, only a single fossil occurrence of this taxon has been documented.
Fusion of dorsal and caudal vertebrae, fused coracoids, and fully ossified limb proximities show that the holotype was a fully grown adult.
The costal ribs likely moved transversely during respiration, allowing the animal to breathe while swimming.
Phylogenetic analyses place Argentinonectes within the elasmosaurid clade Weddellonectia, often as the sister taxon to Chubutinectes.
It belongs to the family Elasmosauridae, which is part of the broader group Weddellonectia.
Overall, Argentinonectes is classified as a reptile.
The type locality of Argentinonectes is the Calafate Formation in Argentina.
It lived during the Late Cretaceous Maastrichtian age.
The Maastrichtian spans from about 72.2 to 66 million years ago.
